column4: Pessimistic concurrency control locks a record as soon as a transaction reads it, so nobody else can change it until the transaction finishes. It is safe when conflicts are frequent but it reduces throughput and can cause deadlocks. Optimistic control lets everyone read without locks and checks a version number or timestamp at commit time, rolling back if someone else changed the row. It works well when conflicts are rare because there is no waiting, but retries become expensive under heavy contention.
Concurrency is very important in modern software. I usually use Docker and Kubernetes to scale services across cloud regions so that transactions do not fail.

In my final year project our login service started failing two days before the demo. I was the backend lead, so fixing it was my responsibility. I checked the logs, found that the database connection pool was exhausted, increased the pool size, added a timeout with retry, and wrote a small load test to confirm the fix. The demo ran without errors and we kept the load test in our repository so it would not happen again.
We had a big bug and everyone was stressed. We tried many things and later it was fixed. It was a good learning for all of us.

A process is a program in execution with its own memory. A thread is a smaller unit inside a process and threads share the same memory, so they are lighter than processes, but sharing memory can cause problems like race conditions.

An index is a data structure like a B-tree that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table, so reads and searches become much faster. The cost is that every insert, update or delete must also update the index, so writes get slower and the index uses extra storage. So we index columns used often in where clauses and joins, but we avoid indexing everything.
